\[\begin{gathered}
 \frac{{{P^0} - {P_s}}}{{{P^0}}} = {x_2} = \frac{{{n_2}}}{{{n_2} + {n_1}}} \approx \frac{{{n_2}}}{{{n_1}}} \\

\end{gathered} \]

q: 1.0 molal solution of which of the following compounds will have the lowest freezing point?
s:
"THIS IS A HIGH WEIGHTAGE TOPIC"
$\Delta {T_f} = i{K_f}\,m$
Since solutions have the same molality, the solution with maximum van’t Hoff factor (i) will have maximum depression in freezing point, i.e., it will have lowest freezing point.

For KCl; i = 2

subject: Chemistry
q:
Which of the following observations indicate(s) colligative properties?
I. A 0.5 M NaBr solution has a higher vapour pressure than 0.5 M BaCl_2.
II. A 0.5 M NaOH solution freezes at a lower temperature than pure water.
III. Pure water freezes at a higher temperature than pure ethanol.
s:
"THIS IS A HIGH WEIGHTAGE TOPIC"
Relative lowering in vapour pressure is a colligative property and it is directly proportional to number of solute particles. 0.5 BaCl_2 (i = 3) will have a greater number of solute particles than 0.5 M NaBr (i = 2). Thus, 0.5 M NaBr will have a higher vapour pressure than 0.5 M BaCl_2.
On addition of non-volatile NaOH to water, the freezing point of the water decreases. This phenomenon is called depression in freezing point, and it is a colligative property.
Pure water freezes at a temperature greater than pure ethanol due to stronger intermolecular forces.

q: The dipole moment of o, p and m-dichlorobenzene will be in the order
s:
[IMAGE NOT CAPTURED] μ = 0 μ = \[\sqrt 3 \]x μ = x
In p-dichlorobenzene, two C-Cl dipoles cancel each other
∴ μ = 0.
In o-dichlorobenzene, the two C-Cl dipoles (say x) are inclined at an angle of 60°. Therefore, according to parallelogram law of forces, the resultant
\[\begin{gathered}
 = \sqrt {{x^2} + {x^2} + 2{x^2} \times \cos {{60}^{\text{o}}}} \\
 = \sqrt {{x^2} + {x^2} + 2{x^2} \times 1/2} = \sqrt {3{x^2}} = \sqrt {3}x \\ 
\end{gathered} \]
In m-dichlorobenzene, the two dipoles are inclined to each other at an angle of 120°, therefore, resultant
\[\begin{gathered}
 = \sqrt {{x^2} + {x^2} + 2{x^2} \times \cos {{120}^{\text{o}}}} \\
 = \sqrt {{x^2} + {x^2} + 2{x^2} \times \left( { - 1/2} \right)} = \sqrt {{x^2}} = x \\ 
\end{gathered} \]
Thus, the decreasing order of dipole moments is o > m > p .

q: The ratio of 1^st, 2^nd and 3^rd ionisation enthalpies of A^–(g) is 1 : 3 : 12. If total energy for the process A^2+(g) $\to$ A^–(g) is –320 kcal/mole, then the 2^nd ionisation enthalpy of A(g) (in kcal/mol) is
s:
"THIS IS A HIGH WEIGHTAGE TOPIC"
 A^–(g) $\to$ A(g) + e–; IE_1 of A^–
A(g) $\to$ A^+(g) + e–; IE_2 of A^–
A^+(g) $\to$ A^2+(g) + e–; IE_3 of A^– = IE_2 of A(g)
Thus, for A^2+(g) $\to$ A^–(g), energy change = – (IE_1 + IE_2 + IE_3)
Let the values of IE_1, IE_2 and IE_3 be x, 3x and 12x respectively.
–16x = –320
x = 20 kcal/mole
Thus, IE_2 of A(g) = IE_3 of A^– = 12x = 240 kcal/mole

n mole of PCl_3 and n mole of Cl_2 are allowed to react at constant temperature T to have a total equilibrium pressure P, as:
PCl_3(g) + Cl_2(g) $ \rightleftharpoons $ PCl_5(g)
If y mole of PCl_5 is formed at equilibrium, find K_P for the given reaction.
s:
"THIS IS A HIGH WEIGHTAGE TOPIC"
 [IMAGE: images/MB002535_1.webp] Total moles at equilibrium = (n – y) + (n – y) + y = 2n – y
Thus, partial pressure of PCl_5 = \[\left( {\frac{y}{{2n - y}}} \right)P\]
Partial pressure of Cl_2 = \[\left( {\frac{{n - y}}{{2n - y}}} \right)P\]
Partial pressure of PCl_3 = \[\left( {\frac{{n - y}}{{2n - y}}} \right)P\]
Thus, \[{K_p} = \frac{{{P_{PC{l_5}}}}}{{{P_{C{l_2}}} \cdot {P_{PC{l_3}}}}} = \frac{{\left( {\frac{y}{{2n - y}}} \right)P}}{{\left( {\frac{{n - y}}{{2n - y}}} \right)P \cdot \left( {\frac{{n - y}}{{2n - y}}} \right)P}} = \] 

$\frac{{(2n - y)y}}{{{{(n - y)}^2}P}}$

q: Sulphide ion in alkaline solution reacts with solid sulphur to form polysulphide ions having formulae \[{S_2}^{2 - },{S_3}^{2 - },{S_4}^{2 - }\] and so on. The equilibrium constant for the formation of \[{S_2}^{2 - }\] is 12 and for the formation of \[{S_3}^{2 - }\] is 132, both from \[S\]and \[{S^{2 - }}\]. What is the equilibrium constant for formation of \[{S_3}^{2 - }\] from \[{S_2}^{2 - }\] and \[S\]?
s:
"THIS IS A HIGH WEIGHTAGE TOPIC"
 Given data –
\[S + {S^{2 - }} \rightleftharpoons {S_2}^{2 - };\,{K_1} = 12\]
\[2S + {S^{2 - }} \rightleftharpoons {S_3}^{2 - };\,{K_2} = 132\]
Required reaction is \[S + {S_2}^{2 - } \rightleftharpoons {S_3}^{2 - };\,{K_3} = ?\]
On reversing the first equation and then adding it to the second equation, we get the required equation.
Thus, \[\,{K_3} = \frac{{{K_2}}}{{{K_1}}} = \frac{{132}}{{12}} = 11\]

 Mass of \[F{e_2}{O_3}\]in the sample \[ = \frac{{55.2}}{{100}} \times 1 = 0.552g\]

\[n = \frac{{6.90}}{{1.1356}} = 6\]

q:
Given standard electrode potentials
$F{e^{ + + }} + 2{e^ - }\, \to \,Fe\,;\,\,\,\,{E^o} = - 0.440\,\,V$
$F{e^{ + + + }} + 3{e^ - }\, \to \,Fe\,;\,\,\,\,{E^o} = - 0.036\,\,V$
The standard electrode potential $({E^o})$ for $F{e^{ 3 + }} + {e^ - } \to \,F{e^{ 2 + }}$ is
s:
"THIS IS A HIGH WEIGHTAGE TOPIC"
 $\Delta {G^o} = - n{E^o}F$
$F{e^{2 + }} + 2{e^ - } \to Fe$…..(i)
$\Delta {G^o} = - 2 \times F \times ( - 0.440\,V) = 0.880\,F$
$F{e^{3 + }} + 3{e^ - } \to Fe$…..(ii)
$\Delta {G^o} = - 3 \times F \times ( - 0.036) = 0.108F$
On subtracting equation (i) from (ii)
$F{e^{3 + }} + {e^ - } \to F{e^{2 + }}$
$\Delta {G^o} = 0.108F - 0.880F = - 0.772F$
${E^o}$ for the reaction $ = - \frac{{\Delta {G^o}}}{{nF}}$ $ = - \frac{{( - \,0.772\,F)}}{{1 \times F}} = + \,0.772\,V$.

Mix a little amount of salt and an equal amount of solid potassium dichromate (K_2Cr_2O_7) in a test tube and add conc.H_2SO_4 to it. Heat the test tube and pass the evolved gas through sodium hydroxide solution. If a yellow solution is obtained, divide the solution into two parts. Acidify the first part with acetic acid and then add lead acetate solution. Formation of a yellow precipitate of lead chromate confirms the presence of chloride ions in the salt. This test is called chromyl chloride test.

CrO_2Cl_2 + 4NaOH⟶Na_2CrO_4 + 2NaCl + 2H_2O

q:
In which of the following processes, the sign of ∆G is negative? Each process involves pure substance ‘A’ whose normal melting and boiling points are 200 K and 300 K respectively.
(i) A(s) $\to$ A(l) at 250 K and 1 atm
(ii) A(l) $\to$ A(s) at 150 K and 1 atm
(iii) A(l) $\to$ A(g) at 300 K and 0.1 atm
(iv) A(l) $\to$ A(g) at 250 K and 2 atm
s:
Normal melting point is the temperature at which the solid and liquid phase are in equilibrium at 1 atm pressure.
Normal boiling point is the temperature at which the liquid and vapour phase are in equilibrium at 1 atm pressure.
(i) Since the temperature is more than the normal melting point, and pressure is the same, the conversion of solid to liquid will occur spontaneously, i.e., ∆G < 0.
(ii) Since the temperature is less than the normal melting point, and pressure is the same, the conversion of liquid to solid will occur spontaneously, i.e., ∆G < 0.
(iii) At lower pressure, the boiling point of the liquid decreases. Thus, the given liquid will boil spontaneously at 300 K and 0.1 atm pressure, i.e., ∆G < 0.
(iv) At higher pressure, the boiling point of the liquid increases. Thus, the given liquid will not boil spontaneously at 250 K and 2 atm pressure, i.e., ∆G > 0.

q:
A source of monochromatic radiation of wavelength 400 nm provides 1000 J of energy in 10 seconds. When this radiation falls on the surface of sodium, \[x \times {10^{20}}\] electrons are ejected per second. Assume that wavelength 400 nm is sufficient for ejection of electron from the surface of sodium metal. The value of x is _______. (Nearest integer)
(\[h = 6.626 \times {10^{ - 34}}Js\])
s:
"THIS IS A HIGH WEIGHTAGE TOPIC"
 Since the incident wavelength is equal to the threshold wavelength of the metal. It means whole of the energy of a photon will be used in ejecting an electron. Thus, the number of electrons ejected per second will be equal to the number of photons striking the metal surface per second.
The energy provided by the given radiation in 10 sec = 1000 J
Thus, the energy provided by the given radiation in 1 sec = 100 J
Now, \[E = \frac{{nhc}}{\lambda } \Rightarrow n = \frac{{E\lambda }}{{hc}}\]
\[ \Rightarrow n = \frac{{100 \times 400 \times {{10}^{ - 9}}}}{{6.626 \times {{10}^{ - 34}} \times 3 \times {{10}^8}}} = 20.12 \times {10^{19}} = 2.012 \times {10^{20}}\]
